intro:
By the end of this track you can say where a JVM's start-up time and memory go, and measure both the way your users and a memory limit see them: time to first request from outside the process, and RSS from the operating system. You can build and check a class data sharing archive on JDK 21 and a Project Leyden AOT cache on JDK 25, and you know the traps that quietly make them useless or, on JDK 25 builds before 25.0.4, run stale code. You can explain what GraalVM native image's closed world costs, write its reachability metadata, and spot static initializers that break when the build runs them. You can write CRaC checkpoint hooks in the right order, and choose between doing nothing, AppCDS, the AOT cache, native image and CRaC for a given service. One picture runs through the whole track, a corner shop that has to open every morning, and so does one program, a small parcel-tracking service.

You need no background in any of this: lesson 1 starts from what happens between typing `java` and the first line of `main`. Install JDK 25, at least 25.0.4, because earlier JDK 25 builds can run old classes from an AOT cache after the JAR changes. The Leyden flags need JDK 24 or 25 and say so wherever they appear. Native image needs GraalVM or Mandrel, and CRaC needs a CRaC-enabled vendor JDK, such as Azul's Zulu CRaC builds on Linux. Those steps are marked optional, and everything else runs on a plain JDK.

The labs live in `labs/startup`, one package per lesson (`workbench.startup.l01` to `l04`). Lessons 1 and 3 are in Java, lessons 2 and 4 in Kotlin, and every sample and demo comes in both languages. Start-up numbers are noisy, so no test measures time or counts all loaded classes. The tests load your classes in fresh class loaders and compare exact sets of class names, check JSON metadata against the GraalVM schema and against what the code really does, and drive a simulated checkpoint. Many demos start a second JVM with the flags you pass in `-Pargs`, because start-up has to be measured on a fresh process, and Gradle runs them on the JDK that runs Gradle. A few Try-its run `java` directly on a JDK 25 against `startup/build/classes/java/demo`. Run `./gradlew :startup:test --tests 'workbench.startup.lNN.*'` from `labs/` until it passes, and `./gradlew :startup:solutionTest` to run the same tests on the reference answers.
cheatsheet:
## The shop, part by part

The track explains start-up with one corner shop that has to open every morning. Each picture fits one idea, and each breaks somewhere: the JVM unpacks lazily, not before opening; a one-line change to a native image means rebuilding the whole stall; and one CRaC photo can wake up as many copies as you like.

| JVM idea | Picture it | Lesson |
|---|---|---|
| creating the VM (`Create VM`) | unlocking the door and switching on the lights | 1 |
| loading and parsing a class; verification | unpacking a box; checking each item against its delivery note | 1 |
| lazy loading; the holder idiom | a box opened only when a customer asks for what's inside; a sealed box in the back room | 1 |
| the interpreter, then the JIT with profiles | looking up every price, then learning the popular items by heart | 1, 4 |
| the program's `started in` line; time to first request | the OPEN sign; the first customer walking out with what they came for | 1 |
| committed memory; resident memory (RSS) | floor space booked; floor actually filled with shelves | 1 |
| the default CDS archive; AppCDS | the shelves that came with the shop; your own goods on shelves kept in the back room | 2 |
| the AOT cache: training, assembly, production | a notebook: one day of noting what you used, an evening writing it up, every morning after | 2 |
| a cache built from another JAR, JDK or GC | last week's shelves: refused since 25.0.4, and a refused cache means no shelves at all | 2 |
| native image and its closed world | a pop-up stall stocked at the factory: it opens at once and sells only what was packed | 3 |
| reachability metadata | the packing list for items customers ask for by name | 3 |
| build-time initialization | signs filled in at the factory, the factory's date included | 3 |
| CRaC checkpoint and restore | a photo of the busy shop, stepped back into later | 4 |
| `beforeCheckpoint` and `afterRestore`, in reverse order | hanging up the phones before the photo; switching off at night in the reverse of the morning's order | 4 |
| many copies restored from one image | ten shops from one photo, every till starting at ticket 42 | 4 |

## Measure first

| Question | Command or tool |
|---|---|
| Where did each class come from? | `java -Xlog:class+load ...`: `source: shared objects file` (archive), `jrt:/` (parsed from the JDK), `file:` (class path), a class name (hidden class) |
| How long did VM creation take? | `-Xlog:startuptime`, last line `Create VM, 0.05 secs`. Nothing about your code |
| What does the user wait for? | Time to first request: launch the process, then ask the service from outside until it answers 200 |
| What is the footprint? | RSS: `ps -o pid,rss,args -p <pid>`, `/proc/<pid>/status` (`VmRSS`, `RssAnon`, `RssFile`). Not `docker stats`, not "heap used" |
| Where inside the JVM did memory go? | `-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary`, then `jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary`. Committed is not resident |

## Class loading and initialization

- Loading parses a class into metaspace, verification checks its bytecode, and `<clinit>` runs on first active use (`new`, a static call, a non-constant static field, reflection that initializes, a subclass).
- Holder idiom: put the expensive static field in a private nested class. Kotlin: a private nested `object`, or `by lazy`. A companion object's properties are static fields of the outer class, and they are built with it.

## Class data sharing (CDS)

| Kind | Commands | Since |
|---|---|---|
| Default archive | on unless `-Xshare:off`; `lib/server/classes.jsa` | JDK 12 |
| Dynamic AppCDS | `-XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=app.jsa`, then `-XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa` | JDK 13 |
| Static AppCDS | `-Xshare:off -XX:DumpLoadedClassList=app.classlist`, `-Xshare:dump -XX:SharedClassListFile=app.classlist -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa`, then `-XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa` | JDK 10 |
| Auto-created | `-XX:+AutoCreateSharedArchive -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa` (not for read-only or throwaway servers) | JDK 19 |

Rules: JARs only (no folders of classes), the same class path or a prefix of it, and a changed JAR is rejected. CDS saves loading and verifying; it doesn't run static initializers or warm up the JIT.

## Leyden AOT cache (final features, no flags to switch them on)

| JDK | What you get |
|---|---|
| 24 | JEP 483: `-XX:AOTMode=record -XX:AOTConfiguration=app.aotconf`, then `-XX:AOTMode=create ... -XX:AOTCache=app.aot`, then `-XX:AOTCache=app.aot` |
| 25 | JEP 514: one step, `-XX:AOTCacheOutput=app.aot`. JEP 515: method profiles |
| 26 | JEP 516: the full cache with any GC, ZGC included |
| 27 | `-XX:AOTMode=required` is the name for `on` |
| 28 (in development) | JEP 544: compiled code in the cache |

- Require **JDK 25.0.4+ or 26.0.2+** (JDK-8377932: earlier builds ran stale classes after the JAR changed). Rebuild the cache with every JAR, in the same build step.
- A cache is tied to the class path, the exact JDK build, the OS and CPU, the GC (on JDK 25) and the module options. A cache the JVM can't use leaves no archive at all, not even the default one: `java -version` then says `mixed mode` without `, sharing`.
- Production: no `AOTMode` (the default `auto` runs without the cache when it doesn't fit). Build checks: `-XX:AOTMode=on` (`required` on 27+) with `-Xlog:aot`, looking for `Opened AOT cache`.
- Quarkus 3.40: `quarkus.package.jar.aot.enabled=true` trains during the integration tests; run `java -XX:AOTCache=app.aot -jar quarkus-run.jar`. On JDK 21: `quarkus.package.jar.aot.type=app-cds`.

## GraalVM native image

```json
{
  "reflection": [
    { "condition": { "typeReached": "tracker.EventDecoder" },
      "type": "tracker.ParcelScanned",
      "methods": [ { "name": "<init>", "parameterTypes": ["java.lang.String", "java.lang.String", "long"] },
                   { "name": "parcelId", "parameterTypes": [] } ] },
    { "type": { "proxy": ["tracker.DepotClient", "java.lang.AutoCloseable"] } }
  ]
}
```

- Needs GraalVM or Mandrel. File: `META-INF/native-image/<groupId>/<artifactId>/reachability-metadata.json`. Schema v1.2.0 top level: `reflection`, `resources`, `foreign`, `comment` only.
- Proxies are ordered interface lists; serialization is `"serializable": true`; a `Class.forName` with a constant argument needs no entry.
- Tracing agent: `java -agentlib:native-image-agent=config-output-dir=<dir> ...`. Strict mode: `--exact-reachability-metadata`, `-XX:MissingRegistrationReportingMode=Exit`.
- Quarkus initializes all classes at build time. Fix one with `quarkus.native.additional-build-args=--initialize-at-run-time=a.B\\,c.D`.
- Quarkus: `@RegisterForReflection` (`targets` for a library's classes, `ignoreNested`, `serialization`), `@RegisterForProxy(targets = ...)` in order, `quarkus.native.resources.includes`.

## CRaC

```bash
java -XX:CRaCCheckpointTo=cr -jar tracker.jar   # start, then warm it up
jcmd tracker.jar JDK.checkpoint                 # read the app's console: jcmd always says success
java -XX:CRaCRestoreFrom=cr                     # restore, already warm
```

- Hooks: `org.crac.Resource` (`beforeCheckpoint`, `afterRestore`), `Core.getGlobalContext().register(r)` in org.crac 1.5.0. Keep `r` in a field: the context holds weak references.
- Order: checkpoint in reverse registration order, restore in registration order. Everyone is told even if one throws; failures arrive as suppressed exceptions on a `CheckpointException`.
- Open files and sockets fail the checkpoint (policy `error`). Socket `reopen` isn't implemented. Recreate per-copy ids and tokens after the restore.
- Builds: Azul Zulu 17, 21 and 25 Linux `-crac-` builds; BellSoft Liberica 17 and 21 CRaC builds. Not in mainline OpenJDK. AWS Lambda SnapStart uses the same hooks.

## Choosing

| Constraint | Pick | Picture it |
|---|---|---|
| Long-running, rarely restarted, nobody waits on start-up | nothing | unpack every morning, it's fine |
| JDK 21, no code changes | dynamic AppCDS built with the program | shelves kept in the back room |
| JDK 25.0.4+, no code changes, full peak throughput | AOT cache trained by integration tests | the shelves plus the notebook |
| Milliseconds to start, or memory per copy, is the limit | native image (about 59% lower peak in Quarkus's benchmark) | the pop-up stall |
| Must start fast and warm, runtime under your control | CRaC or Lambda SnapStart, with hooks | the photo of the busy shop |
recap: Start-up repeats the same work on every launch: create the VM, load, parse and verify each class on first need (818 for a one-class demo on JDK 25, about 1,500 for a 300-class app), run static initializers, interpret until the JIT has profiles, and run any framework's start-up.
Measure what users see: time to first request from outside, and RSS from `ps` or `/proc`. `Create VM`, the program's own `started in`, NMT's committed memory and `docker stats` each miss part of it.
`<clinit>` runs on first active use. The holder idiom (a nested class, or a Kotlin nested `object`) keeps expensive static work off the start-up path; a Kotlin companion object does not.
CDS maps ready-made classes from an archive: the default one for the JDK's classes, AppCDS for yours. It saves loading and verification, not initialization or JIT warm-up.

The AOT cache (final in JDK 24, one step on JDK 25) adds linked classes, resolved lambdas and profiles from a training run. Require JDK 25.0.4+, rebuild it with every JAR, check it in your build, and run production in the default mode.
A training run, an AOT cache and the native-image tracing agent all see only the code paths you exercise, so drive them with production-like traffic.

Native image starts in milliseconds and uses less memory, but has no JIT (lower peak), needs metadata for reflection and proxies, needs GraalVM or Mandrel to build, and runs static initializers at build time in Quarkus.

CRaC restores a warm process from an image, on a CRaC-enabled vendor JDK. Close sockets and files before the checkpoint, reopen them after, mind the hook order and the weak references, and recreate per-copy state.
Default to the JVM with an AOT cache or AppCDS; choose native or CRaC only when start-up or memory per copy is the real limit and you accept their costs.

quiz.q: A new copy of your service logs `started in 0.9s`, but the load balancer only sends it traffic 2.4 s after the process was launched. Which number should you work on, and how do you measure it?
options: The 0.9 s from the log, because it is the service's start-up
The `Create VM` time from `-Xlog:startuptime`
Time from launch to the first 200 from the health check, measured from outside
The time until C2 has compiled the hot methods
quiz.why: Only the outside clock includes everything the load balancer waits for: the launcher, VM creation, class loading, the program's own start-up and the first request. The service's log line starts late and stops early, and `Create VM` stops before your code runs.

quiz.q: In Kotlin, `class DeliveryCalendar { companion object { val holidays = loadHolidays(); fun source() = "national" } }`. A health check calls `DeliveryCalendar.source()`. Is `loadHolidays()` called?
options: No, companion objects are lazy
Yes: `holidays` is a static field of `DeliveryCalendar`, filled when the class is initialized, which this first call triggers
Only on the first access to `holidays`
Only if `holidays` is declared `const`
quiz.why: Kotlin compiles companion properties to static fields of the outer class and fills them in its `<clinit>`. Use a private nested `object` holding `holidays`, or `by lazy`, to build them only when needed.

quiz.q: NMT reports 296 MB committed, 216 MB of it heap, while `VmRSS` is 60 MB. What explains the gap?
options: NMT counts the heap twice
The JVM leaked native memory
RSS doesn't include the Java heap
Committed memory has been requested from the operating system, but most of it, such as a fresh heap, has never been touched, so it isn't resident
quiz.why: Pages become resident only when something touches them. A memory limit counts resident memory, so RSS is the footprint; NMT tells you which part of the JVM asked for what.

quiz.q: On JDK 25, `java -Xshare:off -version` loads 411 classes and none comes from an archive; without the flag, 396 load and 393 are shared. Why does start-up get slower with sharing off?
options: Each class now has to be found, parsed and verified by the JVM instead of being mapped ready-made from `classes.jsa`
The JIT is turned off along with sharing
The heap is smaller
The JVM runs every static initializer twice
quiz.why: The default CDS archive holds the JVM's internal form of about 1,300 JDK classes. Without it every class goes the full way, and the JVM also generates on the spot some classes the archive would have supplied, hence 411 instead of 396.

quiz.q: A build rebuilt `tracker.jar` with a fix and reused last week's `app.aot`. The server runs JDK 25.0.2. What do you expect?
options: A warning, then the fixed code without the cache
The JVM refuses to start
Possibly last week's classes, served from the cache with no error (JDK-8377932)
The fixed code, with the full speed-up
quiz.why: JDK 25.0.0 to 25.0.3 (and 26.0.0 to 26.0.1) didn't check the application's JARs against the cache. 25.0.4 and later warn and run without the cache. Pin 25.0.4 or later, and rebuild the cache with every JAR.

quiz.q: Someone adds `-XX:AOTCache=/srv/app.aot` to every server's `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS`, but the file isn't there. What happens to start-up?
options: Nothing changes: the JVM ignores the flag
It gets slower than with no flag: the JVM runs with no archive at all, not even the default CDS archive
The JVM refuses to start
The JVM writes the cache when it exits
quiz.why: In the default `auto` mode the JVM prints an error and carries on, but with zero archived classes; in this track's run, a one-class program went from 542 shared classes to 0. Only `-XX:AOTMode=on` or `required` makes it stop, and only `-XX:AOTCacheOutput` writes a cache.

quiz.q: Which entry correctly registers a JDK dynamic proxy over `tracker.DepotClient` and `java.io.Closeable` in schema v1.2.0?
options: `{"proxy": [["tracker.DepotClient", "java.io.Closeable"]]}` at the top level
`{"reflection": [{"type": "tracker.DepotClient", "allPublicMethods": true}]}`
A `proxy-config.json` next to the file
`{"reflection": [{"type": {"proxy": ["tracker.DepotClient", "java.io.Closeable"]}}]}`
quiz.why: In v1.2.0 a proxy is a reflection entry whose type is an object with an ordered `proxy` list. The top level allows only `reflection`, `resources`, `foreign` and `comment`, and Quarkus 4.0 doesn't support the legacy separate files. Registering the interface itself doesn't define the proxy class.

quiz.q: A Quarkus native service has `static final String NODE_ID = UUID.randomUUID().toString().substring(0, 8);` in an ordinary class, used to start every event id it writes. Assuming the build succeeds, what do copies started from the same binary see?
options: The same `NODE_ID` in every copy, computed once during the build
A different `NODE_ID` in each copy
`null`
A different value on every read
quiz.why: Quarkus initializes all classes at build time by default, so the initializer runs once in the build and its result is stored in the image heap. Per-copy values belong in code that runs at start-up, or in a class marked `--initialize-at-run-time`.

quiz.q: A service registers its database pool first and its scan listener second with the CRaC global context. The listener forgets to close its queue connection. What happens on `jcmd tracker.jar JDK.checkpoint`?
options: `jcmd` reports an error and the JVM exits
The checkpoint fails under the default `error` policy; the restore hooks run in registration order, and the app's console, not `jcmd`, shows the error
The image is written, and the connection is reopened after the restore
Only the listener's hooks run
quiz.why: Open sockets fail the checkpoint by default. The context still tells everyone (listener, then pool, before; pool, then listener, after), collects the problems in a `CheckpointException`, and the process keeps running. `jcmd` prints success either way.

quiz.q: A company runs 120 small, lightly loaded services on each machine, and memory per copy is what limits how many fit. Slower builds are acceptable. Which option fits best?
options: The JVM with no changes
An AOT cache on JDK 25
A native image for each service
CRaC for each service
quiz.why: Density is native image's strongest case: in Quarkus's benchmark, 95 MiB of RSS against 304 MiB on the JVM and 240 MiB with the AOT cache. Its lower peak throughput matters little for lightly loaded services. CRaC restores a full warm JVM, so it doesn't cut memory.
